chapter: Minton's, Louis Armstrong and the South
title: Dave Tough: friend and model of accompaniment
summary: Clarke recalls his closeness to Dave Tough and Casey on 52nd Street and in Chicago, and admired Tough's steady, supportive drumming over Buddy Rich's rushing.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: : Listen, did Davey Tough come up?
Davey? Oh, that was my man. Davey and Casey.

Oh, I loved them. Davey. He would say, 'That's wonderful, Kenny.' 'That was really wonderful.' You know, he would talk like that. Then he joined -- what was that trumpet player's band? He was in Chicago.
No, no, no. He became quite famous, this trumpet player.
: Well, what color? You mean Muggsy?
No, no. Davey was in Chicago with him, and that's where we used to really hang out together and talk drums all the time.
Well, what kind of trumpet player?
Are you sure it was a trumpet player?
Yeah, I'm sure of that, yeah. I keep thinking -- it's funny how -- if I think about it it all comes back.
When you try to think about it on the spur of the moment, you can't.
But, I can't think. I mean there was Harry James, there was --
No, there was another trumpet player who played kind of like sweet style, you know.
Oh, like that came out of the Goodman band or something. One of those?
This thing is going to stop on us in a minute.
Anyway, Davey Davies was in Chicago, and that's when we really began to talk about --
Well, when you were in Minton's that was earlier than that.
But I mean when we were in Chicago together.
But in New York, we would always be tramping up and down 52nd Street.
And Casey and I would be picking Dave up.
Stuffing him in a cab, sending him to Jersey or somewhere where they lived.
Oh, he was a -- we were really good friends.
I mean it's just one drummer who had -- he was so open.
You know, anything you'd ask him, he would tell you.
Or he would give me his opinion.
No beating around the bush. He would say what he --
: Yeah. There was no subterfuge or anything to have.
No. No. That's what I loved about him.
: And he was a very -- a very intelligent
guy. A very artistic, intelligent guy.

You're telling me. And they used to talk about -- and I used to say -- they would talk about Gene Krupa or Buddy Rich or -- I would say, "Man, have you guys ever heard Dave Tough?" You know. "I'm talking about, now there's a man who really accompanies a band."
That drive. And he kept the beat. Like the time never went up or went down.
I said that's for me. That's the way I want to play, you know. Like Buddy Rich he'd play fast awhile, and then the tempo would get faster and faster, and that's why --
